entry: Type of cyberattack against a computer or network service. Attackers flood a target with superfluous requests or invalid data to overload it and block legitimate requests. In a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack, the traffic comes from many sources, so blocking a single source is insufficient. Criminal DDoS attacks often target banks or [[Credit card|credit card]] payment gateways, and motives include revenge, blackmail and hacktivism. In February 2020, [[Amazon Web Services]] experienced an attack with a peak volume of 2.3 Tb/s.

French philosopher, art critic and writer, and a prominent figure of the [[Age of Enlightenment]]. With [[Jean Le Rond d'Alembert|Jean le Rond d'Alembert]], he co-created the *[[Encyclopédie]]* in 1751 and became its sole editor after d'Alembert left in 1759. Diderot was also its main contributor, writing around 7,000 articles. The work's secular tone angered religious and government authorities, and the Catholic Church banned it in 1758. Diderot struggled financially for most of his career. In 1766 Russian Empress [[Catherine the Great]] bought his 3,000-volume personal library for 15,000 livres and paid him a further thousand livres a year as its custodian. The *Encyclopédie* is considered one of the forerunners of the [[French Revolution]].

Extinct archaic human species or subspecies of Asia. Denisovans ranged across Asia during the Middle to Late Pleistocene, approximately 200,000–32,000 years ago, and most knowledge of them comes from DNA evidence. The first individual was identified in 2010 from mitochondrial DNA extracted from a juvenile finger bone excavated from [[Siberia|Siberian]] Denisova Cave in the [[Altai Mountains]]. Nuclear DNA shows close affinities with [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]]. Other remains come from sites including the [[Tibetan Plateau]], Laos, [[Taiwan]] and [[Yunnan]]. Denisovans interbred with modern humans: Melanesians, Aboriginal Australians and Filipino Negritos carry roughly 5% Denisovan DNA, compared with 0.2% in mainland Asians and Native Americans. In June 2025 the [[Harbin]] cranium, earlier named *Homo longi*, was identified as Denisovan. Their taxonomy remains unsettled: they may be a new species of [[Homo]] or an archaic subspecies of *Homo sapiens*.

Nordic country in northern Europe (pop., 2025: over 6 million). The Kingdom of Denmark, or Danish Realm, also includes the autonomous [[Faroe Islands]] and [[Greenland]] in the North Atlantic. Metropolitan Denmark consists of the Jutland peninsula and an archipelago of 406 islands, lying between the [[North Sea]] and the [[Baltic Sea]]. The capital, [[Copenhagen]], is on [[Zealand]]. Denmark remained neutral in World War I, but a German invasion in April 1940 ended its neutrality in World War II, and it was liberated in May 1945. In 1973 Denmark joined what is now the [[European Union]] but kept its own currency, the krone. It is a developed country with a high standard of living and robust social welfare policies, and it was the first country to legally recognize same-sex partnerships. Denmark is a founding member of NATO and the [[United Nations]].

American actor, filmmaker, photographer and visual artist. He is considered one of the key figures of the [[New Hollywood]] era. He appeared in two films that made [[James Dean]] famous, *Rebel Without a Cause* and *Giant*. His directorial debut, *Easy Rider* (1969), which he co-wrote, won a [[Cannes Film Festival|Cannes]] award for Best Debut. He became typecast as disturbed outsiders in films such as *Apocalypse Now* (1979) and *[[Blue Velvet (film)|Blue Velvet]]* (1986).

American computer scientist. With Ken Thompson, he created the operating system [[Unix]] and the programming languages B and [[C (programming language)|C]]. Ritchie graduated from [[Harvard University]] in 1963 with degrees in physics and applied mathematics. He joined [[Bell Labs]] in 1967 and retired in 2007 as head of System Software Research at Lucent Technologies. In 1970 Brian Kernighan suggested the name "Unix", a pun on "Multics", the system they had worked on. Ritchie also contributed to the operating systems Plan 9 and Inferno. C influenced languages including [[C++]] and [[Java (programming language)|Java]], and Ritchie co-wrote *The C Programming Language* with Brian Kernighan.

American former basketball player and professional wrestler. Renowned for his defensive and rebounding ability, he played in the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA) for the Detroit Pistons, [[Chicago Bulls]], San Antonio Spurs, [[Los Angeles Lakers]] and Dallas Mavericks, and won five NBA championships. He led the NBA in rebounds per game for a record seven consecutive years. He fought alongside [[Hulk Hogan]] in the main event of two *Bash at the Beach* pay-per-views. He also drew attention for visits to [[North Korea]] and for befriending its leader [[Kim Jong Un]] in 2013.

Mass per unit volume of a substance, usually symbolized ρ. It is calculated as ρ = m/V, where m is mass and V is volume. Density is an intensive property: adding more of a substance increases its mass but not its density. Different materials usually have different densities, which matter for [[Buoyancy]], purity and packaging. [[Osmium]] is the densest known element at standard conditions for temperature and pressure. Density varies with temperature and pressure, far more for gases than for solids and liquids. Relative density, or specific gravity, compares a material with water, so a value below one means the substance floats. In a well-known but probably apocryphal tale, [[Archimedes]] was asked to detect whether a goldsmith had substituted a cheaper [[Alloy|alloy]] in a gold wreath, and is said to have measured the wreath's volume by the rise of water.

Dental treatment to restore the function, integrity and form of a [[Tooth|tooth]] lost to decay, trauma or wear. There are two broad categories. Direct restorations are placed and shaped inside a cleaned cavity in a single visit, while indirect restorations such as inlays and onlays are made outside the mouth and cemented in. Direct fillings commonly use amalgam, a [[Alloy|metal alloy]], or tooth-colored composite and glass ionomer, while indirect restorations may use [[Ceramic|ceramics]], metal alloys or [[Porcelain]] for greater durability. Evidence of tooth filling dates to the Paleolithic, when bitumen was used to fill a tooth in Italy about 13,000 years ago. Preparation involves cutting away decay and unsupported enamel, which is brittle, before the material is placed.

Branch of [[Medicine|medicine]] focused on the teeth, gums and mouth. Also called dental medicine or oral medicine, it covers the study, diagnosis, prevention and treatment of diseases of the mouth, chiefly of the teeth and oral mucosa. Its history is older than written history, with rich evidence from 7,000 BC on, and it is thought to have been the first specialization in medicine to develop its own accredited degree. The practitioner is the dentist, who works with a team that may include dental assistants, dental hygienists and dental technicians. Most treatments prevent or treat the two most common oral diseases, dental caries (tooth decay) and periodontal disease. Common procedures include restorations, extractions, root canal treatment and [[Dentures|dentures]]. Evidence-based practice also considers systemic diseases such as [[Diabetes]], [[Cancer]] and [[HIV/AIDS]], which can affect the mouth.

Prosthetic devices that replace missing teeth, also called false teeth. Dentures are supported by the surrounding soft and hard tissues of the mouth. Conventional dentures are removable, while others are bonded or clasped to natural teeth or dental implants. They improve chewing, support the lips and cheeks, and correct the collapsed appearance caused by tooth loss. Replacing front teeth helps people speak more clearly, and improved looks and speech can boost [[Self-esteem|self-esteem]]. Denture stomatitis, an inflammation of the tissue under the denture, is common among wearers and is caused mainly by *Candida albicans* (90%) together with bacteria. Mouth ulceration, often caused by poorly fitting dentures, is the most common lesion in people with dentures. Tooth loss most often results from periodontal disease and [[Tooth decay]].

City (pop., 2020: 715,522), capital of [[Colorado]], U.S. Denver lies in the South Platte River valley, just east of the Front Range of the [[Rocky Mountains]]. It was founded in 1858 at the confluence of Cherry Creek and the South Platte River during the Gold Rush era, and was named after James W. Denver, governor of the [[Kansas]] Territory at the time. It is nicknamed the "Mile High City" for its official elevation of one mile (5,280 feet). Denver is the 19th-most populous city in the United States. Its ten-county metropolitan area, with 3.1 million residents, is the economic and cultural center of the Front Range Urban Corridor, and the city hosts the headquarters of eight Fortune 500 firms.

American actor and film producer. He first came to prominence in the [[NBC]] medical drama *St. Elsewhere* (1982–1988). He won [[Academy Awards]] for Best Supporting Actor for *Glory* (1989), in which he played an [[American Civil War]] soldier, and for Best Actor for *Training Day* (2001). On Broadway he won a Tony Award for Best Actor in a Play for *Fences* (2010). In 2020 *[[The New York Times]]* named him the greatest actor of the 21st century.

Class of normative [[Ethics|ethical]] theories. These theories judge an action by whether it is right or wrong under a set of duties, rules or principles, rather than by its consequences. They are commonly contrasted with [[Utilitarianism]] and other consequentialist theories. The term was given its current sense by C. D. Broad in his 1930 book *Five Types of Ethical Theory*. [[Immanuel Kant|Kant]] argued that only a good will is good without qualification, and that a person with a good will acts from duty. His categorical imperative requires acting only on maxims that could become universal law, and treating humanity "never simply as a means, but always at the same time as an end."

English [[Electronic music|electronic]] band formed in Basildon, Essex, in 1980. With Vince Clarke as primary songwriter, the band released its debut album, *Speak & Spell*, in 1981. After Clarke left at the end of that year, Martin Gore became chief songwriter. *Violator* (1990) reached number 7 on the Billboard 200. The band was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2020, and since the death of Andy Fletcher in 2022, Dave Gahan and Gore have continued as a duo.

Dissociative disorder marked by persistent feelings of depersonalization or derealization. Depersonalization is a sense of detachment from oneself, as if one were an outside observer of one's thoughts or body. Derealization is detachment from one's surroundings, which may seem foggy, dreamlike or visually distorted. The disorder is thought to be caused largely by interpersonal trauma, such as early childhood abuse. A diagnosis requires that the symptoms be persistent and cause marked distress or impairment. About 1–2% of the general population are affected at some point.

Mental state of low mood and aversion to activity. It affects about 3.5% of the global population, or about 280 million people worldwide, as of 2020. Symptoms can include sadness, hopelessness, difficulty concentrating, changes in sleep or appetite, and suicidal thoughts. Depression can be a normal temporary reaction to events such as bereavement, or a symptom of disorders such as [[Major depressive disorder]], [[Bipolar disorder]] and [[Dysthymia]]. It is also a symptom of some physical diseases and a side effect of some drugs and medical treatments.

Cycle of four German-language music dramas composed by [[Richard Wagner]]. Wagner wrote the libretto and music from 1848 to 1874 and called the cycle a *Bühnenfestspiel* (stage festival play). The works draw loosely on Norse sagas and the *[[Nibelungenlied]]*. They comprise *Das Rheingold* (The Rhinegold), *Die Walküre* (The [[Valkyrie]]), *Siegfried* and *Götterdämmerung* (Twilight of the Gods). A full performance takes about 15 hours over four nights. The cycle was first performed as a whole at the first Bayreuth Festival in 1876, beginning with *Das Rheingold* on August 13 and ending with *Götterdämmerung* on August 17.

American Latin and [[Ballroom dance|ballroom]] dancer, choreographer, actor and singer. From 2007 to 2016 he was a professional dancer on ABC's *Dancing with the Stars*, winning a record six times with his celebrity partners. He received 14 Primetime Emmy Award nominations for Outstanding Choreography, winning four. He was a judge on NBC's *World of Dance* from 2017 to 2020, and became a judge on *Dancing with the Stars* beginning with its 29th season. Since September 2025 he has hosted *Extra*.

English actor. He was a founding member of the National Theatre under [[Laurence Olivier]]. His Shakespearean roles include *[[Hamlet]]*, *[[Macbeth]]* and *[[King Lear]]*. He played [[Claudius]] in the [[BBC]] series *I, Claudius* (1976), winning a British Academy Television Award for Best Actor. He won a Tony Award for Best Actor in a Play for Benedick in *[[Much Ado About Nothing]]* (1985), and was knighted by Queen [[Elizabeth II]] in 1994 for services to theater.

American former [[Baseball|baseball]] shortstop and executive. He spent his entire 20-year career with the [[New York Yankees]], winning five [[World Series]] titles. He was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 2020 with 396 of 397 possible votes, the second-highest percentage in [[Major League Baseball]] history. He was the Yankees' captain from 2003 to 2014 and finished with 3,465 hits. He was chief executive and part owner of the Miami Marlins from 2017 to 2022.

Military junta of [[Ethiopia]], 1974–1987. Officially the Provisional Military Administrative Council, the Derg overthrew Emperor [[Haile Selassie]] in September 1974 and in March 1975 abolished the monarchy and established a communist state. Under Mengistu Haile Mariam, chairman from 1977, it carried out the Red Terror, a campaign of political repression in which tens of thousands were imprisoned and executed without trial. The Derg itself estimated more than a million deaths during its time in power from the 1983–1985 famine. It fell in May 1991 to the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front, ending the [[Ethiopian Civil War|civil war]].

Instantaneous rate of change of a [[Function (mathematics)|function]]'s output with respect to its input. For a function of one variable, the derivative at a point is the slope of the tangent line to the graph there, and the tangent is the best linear approximation of the function near that point. Derivatives are defined as a [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]], and the process of finding one is called [[Differential calculus|differentiation]]. In Leibniz notation, named after [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]], a derivative is written as a ratio of differentials. In physics, the first derivative of position with respect to time is velocity, and the second is [[Acceleration|acceleration]]. For functions of several variables, the derivative generalizes to the Jacobian matrix, which reduces to the [[Gradient|gradient]] vector for real-valued functions.

Type of financial [[Contract|contract]] between a buyer and a seller. Its value depends on an underlier, such as a commodity, stock, bond, currency, interest rate or price index. Each derivative specifies the underlier, a future act such as a sale or purchase, a price, and a future date. Derivatives are used to hedge against price movements, to speculate, or to gain access to assets that are hard to trade. Common types include forwards, futures, options and swaps. The oldest recorded example, attested by [[Aristotle]], is a contract for [[Olive|olives]] made by the Greek philosopher Thales, who made a profit from it. After the [[2008 financial crisis]], there was increased pressure to move derivatives to exchanges.

Branch of [[Medicine|medicine]] dealing with the skin and the [[Integumentary system|integumentary system]]. It has both medical and surgical aspects. A dermatologist is a specialist physician who has completed about four years of advanced training beyond medical school. Common conditions include inflammatory diseases, infections, cancers, hair loss and cosmetic problems. Life-threatening emergencies include serious [[Burn|burns]], angioedema, necrotizing fasciitis and Stevens–Johnson syndrome. Treatments include systemic and topical medications, surgery, radiation, cryosurgery and laser therapy. The word was first attested in English in 1819, derived from the Greek *derma*, meaning skin. In 1708 the first great school of dermatology was established at the Hôpital Saint-Louis in Paris.
